subject: Radiology
content: Diagnostic imaging supports screening, diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, image-guided procedures, and follow-up. Imaging should be selected according to the clinical question, patient factors, available resources, and safety considerations.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Medical imaging includes conventional radiography, fluoroscopy, angiography, computed tomography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, mammography, densitometry, dental radiology, diagnostic nuclear medicine, hybrid imaging such as PET-CT and PET-MR, and interventional radiology.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiography uses X-rays to create projection images of body structures. It is widely used because it is relatively accessible and can answer many common clinical questions, especially involving the chest and bones.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiographic interpretation requires systematic assessment of image quality, relevant anatomy, and patterns of abnormality. WHO diagnostic imaging materials emphasize pattern recognition and structured interpretation of radiographs.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic anatomy and interpretation of the chest
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Chest radiography is a major diagnostic imaging examination for evaluating the lungs, pleura, heart and mediastinum, and other thoracic structures. Interpretation should use a systematic approach and correlate imaging findings with the clinical context.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic anatomy and interpretation of the chest
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Computed tomography uses X-rays and computer processing to produce cross-sectional images. CT can provide detailed anatomical information and is used across many clinical settings, but radiation exposure should be justified and optimized.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: CT is used for evaluation of many conditions, including trauma, acute neurological presentations, thoracic disease, abdominal disease, vascular conditions, and cancer staging. The appropriate protocol depends on the clinical question.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Ultrasound creates images using high-frequency sound waves rather than ionizing radiation. It is useful for examining many soft tissues and organs and is particularly valuable where portable, accessible imaging is needed.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Ultrasound can be used to assess abdominal and pelvic organs, pregnancy, vascular structures, and other soft tissues. Its usefulness depends on the body region, clinical question, operator skill, and imaging conditions.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Magnetic resonance imaging uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency signals to produce detailed images without ionizing radiation. It is particularly useful for many soft-tissue and neurological imaging questions.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: MRI selection depends on the clinical question, patient factors, equipment availability, and safety screening. MRI is different from X-ray and CT because it does not use ionizing radiation.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Mammography is an X-ray-based imaging technique used in breast imaging and can contribute to breast cancer screening and diagnostic evaluation. Because it uses ionizing radiation, appropriate justification and optimization are important.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics; Radiation and health
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Fluoroscopy provides real-time X-ray imaging and can support diagnostic and image-guided procedures. Because it uses ionizing radiation, exposure should be justified and optimized for patients and staff.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Angiography uses imaging to evaluate blood vessels and can be combined with image-guided interventions. It is part of conventional and interventional radiology services.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Interventional radiology uses imaging guidance to perform minimally invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures. Imaging guidance can include fluoroscopy, ultrasound, CT, or other modalities selected for the procedure.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Diagnostic nuclear medicine uses radiopharmaceuticals to obtain information about physiological or functional processes. WHO identifies nuclear medicine, PET, and SPECT among medical imaging modalities.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Hybrid imaging combines functional or molecular information with anatomical imaging. Examples include PET-CT and PET-MR, which integrate different types of information to support diagnosis, staging, and follow-up in selected conditions.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiological examinations using ionizing radiation should be justified so that the expected clinical benefit outweighs the radiation risk. Referral criteria can help clinicians select appropriate imaging examinations.
source: World Health Organization - Justification and optimization in medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Optimization aims to obtain the information needed for clinical care while minimizing unnecessary radiation exposure. Optimization applies to patients, health workers, and other people who may be exposed during medical uses of ionizing radiation.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Medical radiation safety includes protection of patients undergoing radiological procedures as well as carers, comforters, research volunteers, health professionals, and members of the public. Safety requires a systematic approach to balancing benefits and risks.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Children can be more sensitive to radiation risks, making justification and optimization particularly important when imaging children with ionizing radiation. Imaging protocols should be appropriate to the patient and clinical question.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation and health
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. X-rays and gamma rays are forms of ionizing electromagnetic radiation and are used in several medical imaging applications.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiation protection also addresses occupational exposure of healthcare professionals performing radiological procedures. Safe practice requires appropriate systems, training, monitoring, and optimization of exposure.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: The choice of imaging examination should begin with the clinical question and consider the diagnostic value, patient-specific factors, risks, available expertise, and resources. Imaging should not be selected solely because a modality is technologically advanced.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Useful radiological interpretation depends on adequate image quality and appropriate technique. Technical factors, patient positioning, motion, and the selected imaging protocol can affect the quality and interpretability of an examination.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic technique and projections
license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for the cited WHO work; this record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiological findings should be interpreted in the context of the patient's clinical presentation and the question that prompted imaging. Imaging is one component of diagnostic assessment rather than a substitute for clinical evaluation.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Ethical medical imaging includes patient-centered care, appropriate use of imaging, radiation protection, professional responsibility, and safety culture. Ethical practice should align imaging benefits with patient safety.
source: World Health Organization - Ethics and medical radiological imaging
license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for the cited WHO work; this record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiology services should be matched to the needs and capabilities of the healthcare setting. WHO emphasizes effective use of available imaging resources, especially where equipment and trained personnel are limited.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: A medical imaging service requires appropriate equipment, trained personnel, infrastructure, protocols, quality systems, and safety practices. The complexity of services should be appropriate for the healthcare level.
source: World Health Organization - WHO list of priority medical devices for cancer management
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiation safety culture involves actions and systems that improve protection and safety for patients and personnel involved in medical imaging. It includes risk assessment, communication, justification, optimization, and prevention of unintended exposure.
source: World Health Organization - Enhancing radiation safety in health care
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Imaging plays an important role in the evaluation of trauma. The appropriate modality depends on the suspected injury, clinical stability, body region, urgency, and available resources.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostic imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Medical imaging contributes to cancer detection, diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and follow-up. Different modalities provide complementary anatomical or functional information.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Imaging is important in the evaluation of neurological disease. CT and MRI provide different types of anatomical information and are selected according to the clinical question, urgency, patient factors, and availability.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Thoracic imaging can evaluate the lungs, pleura, heart, mediastinum, and related structures. Chest radiography remains an important imaging examination, while CT, ultrasound, and MRI may provide additional information in selected clinical situations.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic anatomy and interpretation of the chest
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Imaging during pregnancy should be selected according to the clinical need and safety considerations. When ionizing radiation is involved, justification and optimization are important to minimize unnecessary exposure.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Pediatric imaging requires attention to patient-specific risks and benefits. For examinations using ionizing radiation, protocols should be justified and optimized because children require particular consideration in radiation protection.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation and health
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: A systematic approach to image interpretation helps reduce missed findings. For radiographs, this includes assessing technical adequacy, reviewing relevant anatomical structures, identifying abnormal patterns, and relating findings to the clinical question.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic anatomy and interpretation of the chest
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Pattern recognition is an important component of radiological interpretation. Learners should connect imaging patterns with anatomy and clinical context rather than relying on isolated visual features.
source: World Health Organization - Radiographic anatomy and interpretation of the chest
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Different imaging modalities provide different types of information. Conventional radiology, CT, ultrasound, MRI, nuclear medicine, and hybrid imaging should be selected based on the diagnostic or procedural objective and the balance of benefits, risks, and resources.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiation safety programs should include measures to prevent accidental or unintended exposure. Risk assessment, appropriate procedures, staff training, communication, and safety systems are important components of medical radiation protection.
source: World Health Organization - Enhancing radiation safety in health care
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Access to safe, effective, and quality-assured diagnostics is an important part of health systems. Imaging services contribute to prevention, screening, diagnosis, case management, monitoring, and surveillance.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Medical imaging using ionizing radiation should balance diagnostic or therapeutic benefit against potential radiation risk. A systematic radiation protection approach seeks to preserve clinical benefits while minimizing unnecessary exposure.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Appropriate imaging requires consideration of the patient's needs, expected diagnostic value, potential harms, and alternatives. Ethical practice supports patient-centered decisions and avoids unnecessary examinations.
source: World Health Organization - Ethics and medical radiological imaging
license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO for the cited WHO work; this record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Imaging can be used for follow-up and monitoring of disease or response to treatment. Follow-up examinations should have a clinical purpose and should use appropriate modality and protocol for the question being assessed.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Medical imaging provides anatomical or functional information that can complement history, examination, laboratory tests, and other investigations. It should be interpreted as part of an integrated diagnostic process.
source: World Health Organization - Diagnostics
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Ultrasound and MRI are major medical imaging techniques that do not use ionizing radiation. Their appropriate use depends on the clinical question, patient characteristics, availability, and technical limitations.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiography, fluoroscopy, CT, mammography, and many nuclear medicine procedures involve ionizing radiation. Their use should follow appropriate justification and optimization principles.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation and health
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: High-quality imaging services require suitable equipment, trained personnel, appropriate protocols, and systems for safety and quality. Service organization should support reliable diagnostic information while minimizing avoidable risk.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiation protection in medical settings also considers exposure of members of the public. Facility design, controlled procedures, and appropriate safety systems help minimize unnecessary exposure.
source: World Health Organization - Radiation protection and safety in medical uses of ionizing radiation
license: WHO/IAEA/ILO/PAHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.

subject: Radiology
content: Radiology encompasses diagnostic and image-guided applications across multiple imaging modalities. Modern medical imaging supports diagnosis, treatment planning, interventions, and follow-up across many clinical specialties.
source: World Health Organization - Strengthening medical imaging
license: WHO source; source-specific reuse terms apply. This record is an original paraphrase with attribution.
